text:
Droit de la famille — 191353

2019 QCCS 2913

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-12-280631-056

DATE:

July 8
th
, 2019

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

CAROL COHEN, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

Y. M.

Plaintiff

v.

P. L.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

on Motions to vary accessory measures

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The Court is seized with motions to vary
accessory measures presented by the self-represented parents of four children. Plaintiff
Y. M. (the “Mother”) and Defendant P. L. (the “Father”) were divorced by
judgment rendered on March 30
th
, 2007 (the “Divorce
judgment”). As will be seen below, the Court homologated several consent
agreements signed by the parties, including one dated July 10
th
,
2007 concerning custody, child support and spousal support, which is at the
heart of the present case. In their motions, the parties are both asking the
Court to vary the terms of this final consent agreement of 2007, albeit in very
different ways.

Facts and proceedings
to date

[
2
]

The parties were married in 1991. They are the
parents of four children – X, born in November 1993 and presently 25 years old;
Y, born in July 1995, who is 24 years old; Z, born in December 1999, 19
years old; and A, born in May 2002, 17 years old. At the time of the
marriage, the Mother was 20 years old and the Father was 30.

[
3
]

The Mother worked in the home throughout the
marriage, although she is now a real estate agent, living with a new partner
for several years. The Mother’s declared revenues have ranged from $57,131 in
2013 to $25,963 in 2018, exclusive of spousal support which ceased in July
2012, as seen below. The Father worked and still works as a professor of
accounting at [University A]. His declared annual income since 2013 has ranged
from approximately $200,000 to $282,050 in 2019.

[
4
]

The parties separated in 2004, when the children
were still very young. On August 4
th
, 2005, the Mother filed an
originating action in divorce in the present file along with a motion for
provisional measures. She claimed spousal support and child support based upon
a Schedule I indicating revenues of $246,500 for the Father and $7,000 for
herself.

[
5
]

On August 11
th
, 2005, the parties signed
an interim agreement (the “2005 Agreement”) which was confirmed by the Court on
that same day. They agreed to have “
joint split custody
” of the
children, who were to alternate between the parents’ houses on a weekly basis
each Friday. The Mother was given exclusive possession of the former common
domicile in City A and the Father agreed to pay spousal support of $4,000 per
month as well as child support of $1,753 per month, calculated pursuant to a
Schedule I filed by the Father which indicated an annual income of
$183,000 per year for him, and an annual income of $10,000 for the Mother. This
child support included “
$6,500 per annum relating to the nanny commencing
August 1
st
, 2005
”, which nanny was to “
travel and accompany
the children between homes
”. The proof shows that this was never done, as
discussed below. The parties also agreed to split the cost of school supplies
and uniforms which would be purchased by the Mother and reimbursed to her
within 5 days of receipt of each claim – once again, this proved to be
problematic from the outset.

[
6
]

Despite the 2005 Agreement, the proceedings have
continued apace throughout most of the last 14 years.

[
7
]

Indeed, the Father presented his first motion
for provisional measures only 3 months after the signing of the 2005
Agreement, on November 18
th
, 2005, (“Father’s 2005 Motion”), in
which he conceded that the “
shared custody
” should continue but asked that
the Court determine his “
obligation to pay spousal support taking into
account Plaintiff’s obligation to take the appropriate steps now towards
attaining her autonomy and to contribute financially to her own support and the
support of the children and thereby to lessen the financial burden on Defendant

”.

[
8
]

The Father’s 2005 Motion was postponed several
times over the following two years and was finally made presentable in March
2007, concurrently with the Mother’s divorce proceedings and her amended motion
for provisional measures. Numerous interim judgments were rendered in
anticipation of the hearing on the parties’ respective motions for provisional
measures and on the divorce action.

[
9
]

The following is a partial summary of the
proceedings and judgments filed since 2005, to date.

[
10
]

On November 23
rd
, 2005, Justice
Ginette Piché confirmed that an amount of $28,003.38 was owing by the Father to
the Mother in reimbursement of school fees and books and ordered that this sum
be reimbursed to the Mother by December 2
nd
, 2005. The Father’s request
to postpone the hearing on the motions for provisional measures was granted and
the case was postponed, first until December 14
th
, 2005 and then
until March 2006.

[
11
]

On March 20
th
, 2006, the Mother presented
an amended motion for provisional measures, asking for joint custody, child
support in accordance with the guidelines, maintenance of the spousal support
without a term, schooling expenses and a provision for costs,
inter alia
.

[
12
]

On May 16
th
, 2006, the Father filed a
contestation to the divorce action, asking for cancellation of the spousal
support and/or the imposition of a term. He also filed an amended motion for
provisional measures on June 1
st
, 2006, asking
inter alia

that the children be moved from private schools to public schools for reasons
of cost of schooling and that they be assessed by an expert of his choice. He
did not ask for a modification of the shared custody provisions in the previous
consents and judgments, which is significant given the motions currently pending
before the Court.

[
13
]

On June 26
th
, 2006, the parties
signed a new partial consent agreement (the “2006 Agreement”), which left in
place the shared or “
split
” custody and which made arrangements for the
summer of 2006, given the Father’s annual summer trip of several weeks to give lectures
in [Country A], allowing for the Mother to have the children along with the
nanny while he was away, as appears from the following extracts of the 2006
Agreement:

7. Regarding the continuation of
the existing split custody arrangement:

a) the parties will attempt to
improve their communication regarding the children;

b) the parties undertake to help
each other out by taking the children during the other’s week of custody if
necessary and subject to their respective availabilities; until Plaintiff
obtains remunerative employment she will make every effort to render herself available
when called upon;

[…]

8. Defendant reserves his right to
request his own expertise for the purpose of determining whether it is in the
best interest of the children to continue the current split custody
arrangement; Plaintiff reserves the right to contest Defendant’s demand for an
expertise and to make such other demands in respect of the question of
expertises she deems necessary.

[
14
]

This 2006 Consent did not resolve the parties’
differences. Indeed, the testimony indicates that the children remained in the
Father’s home with the nanny, who refused to care for them at the Mother’s
residence.

[
15
]

Moreover, the parties each continued to contest
the other’s motion for provisional measures, which motions were initially scheduled
to be heard for three days in November 2006 and then postponed until March 2007
on November 22
nd
, 2006, by Justice Nicole Bénard, who also joined the
motions for provisional measures with the merits of the divorce, as appears
from the following extracts of her judgment:

Considérant que les représentations
des procureurs sont à l’effet que pour disposer du présent litige sur le fond,
ils n’ont besoin que d’une heure additionnelle;

Considérant que les questions en
litige aux mesures provisoires sont les mêmes sur le fond;

Considérant qu’il est dans
l’intérêt de la justice et des parties de fixer la cause pour trois jours afin
qu’il soit disposé du présent dossier;

Le Tribunal autorise le maitre des
rôles à fixer la cause pour audition sur mesures provisoires et au fond sur le
rôle de pratique du 2.01;

Considérant que les seules
questions en litige quant au partage du patrimoine familial sont la valeur des
meubles meublants et la valeur du véhicule automobile et son exclusion;

Cause
fixée pour audition les 26, 27 et 28 mars 2007, salle 2.01 à 9hrs;

[
16
]

On March 26
th
, 2007, Justice Pepita Capriolo
was seized with the merits of the divorce action as well as with the parties’
respective amended motions for provisional measures. At the time, both parties
were represented by counsel, the Mother by Me Linda Schacter and the
Father by Me Andrew Heft.

[
17
]

On March 29
th
, 2007, as the hearing
before Justice Capriolo was not yet completed, the parties signed a new partial
consent on accessory measures (the “2007 Partial Consent”), in which they settled
several questions pending with respect to accessory measures, including
distribution of their RRSPs; the Father’s pension plan (which he retained);
division of insurance proceeds received by the Father; and a final payment of
$16,350 by the Father to the Mother, representing a full and final division of
family patrimony and moveables. Justice Capriolo rendered a Divorce Judgment on
March 30
th
, 2007, homologating this 2007 Partial consent and continuing
the case with respect to child custody, child and spousal support until July 12
th
, 2007,
recommending in the Divorce Judgment that the parties “
undergo serious and
urgent parental coaching
”.

[
18
]

On July 10
th
, 2007, the parties
signed a final consent with respect to custody, child support and spousal
support (the “2007 Final Consent”) which was homologated by Justice Capriolo on
July 12
th
, 2007; this Final Consent, at the heart of the present
litigation, reads as follows:

CONSENT AGREEMENT

WHEREAS there are four children
born issue of the marriage (the “Children”), namely:

X,
born [...] 1993

Y, born [...]

1995

Z, born [...] 1999

A, born [...]

2002

WHEREAS judgement of divorce was
rendered on March 30, 2007 by the Honourable Justice Pepita Capriola;

WHEREAS the issues of child
custody, spousal and child support remain pending before the court;

WHEREAS the Plaintiff is
unemployed, but is actively seeking employment;

WHEREAS the parties wish to enter
into an agreement settling the issue of custody, child and spousal support;

WHEREAS the present Consent
Agreement will take effect as of August 1
st
2007, the Defendant
agreeing to continue paying the Plaintiff both the child and spousal according
to the interim judgement of August 5
th
2005 until July 31
st
2007;

AND THE PARTIES AGREE AS FOLLOWS:

1.          THE PREAMBLE

1.1        That the preamble hereto
is true and correct and forms an integral of the present Agreement;

2.
JOINT CUSTODY

2.1
The Plaintiff and the
Defendant shall have joint custody of the Children, each party to consult the
other prior to making any major decisions concerning the health care,
education, religion and organized activities regarding the Children;

BASIC SCHEDULE

2.2        That as a basic
schedule, the Children’s time shall be shared between the Plaintiff and the
Defendant as follows:

2.2.1     The Children shall be
with the Defendant every Monday morning to Friday after school;

2.2.2     That for the weekend
periods, and on an eight (8) week cycle, the Children shall be with the
Plaintiff and the Defendant as follows:

2.2.2.1  Weekends one, three and
six: With the Defendant from Friday after school to Monday morning;

2.2.2.2  Weekends two, five and
seven: With the Plaintiff from Friday after school to Monday morning, the
Children to be picked up at school or at the Defendant’s residence and to be
brought back directly to school;

2.2.2.3  Weekend four, from Friday
after school to Monday morning: The two younger Children, Z and A will be with
the Plaintiff and the two older Children X and Y shall be with the Defendant;

2.2.2.4  Weekend eight, from Friday
after school to Monday morning: The two older Children, X and Y will be with
the Plaintiff and the two younger Children, Z and A, shall be with the
Defendant;

PEDAGOGICAL DAYS

2.3        That until such time as
the Plaintiff is working, the Children will be with the Plaintiff on all pedagogical
days, the Defendant undertaking to bring the Children to the Plaintiff in the
morning and the Plaintiff undertaking to bring the Children back to the
Defendant in the evening;

SICK DAYS

2.4        That until such time as
the Plaintiff is working, the Children will be with the Plaintiff on all sick
days that occur on a school day, the Defendant undertaking to bring the sick
child to the Plaintiff;

STATUTORY HOLIDAYS

2.5        That where a statutory
holiday falls on a Friday or a Monday, (excluding Christmas and New Year), the
party having weekend access will have the Children with him/her for the
statutory holiday. All other statutory holidays will be shared between the
parties, on an alternating basis;

HOLIDAYS

2.6        That as a holiday
schedule the Minor Children’s time shall be shared as follows;

2.6.1     CHRISTMAS/NEW YEAR

2.6.1.1  The Christmas/New Year
school holiday will be divided between the parties, one half each, the one half
to include Christmas or New Year, alternating each year;

2.6.1.2  That in the event that
either party wishes to travel with the Children, the parties agree to modify
the schedule accordingly, acting reasonably;

2.6.2     SPRING/MID WINTER BREAK

2.6.2.1  That until such time as
the Plaintiff is working, the Children will be with the Plaintiff for the
Spring/Mid Winter school break;

2.6.2.2  Once the Plaintiff is
working, the Plaintiff will only take the Children for all or part of the
Spring/Mid Winter break if she is able to have time off from work;

2.6.3     [RELIGION A] HOLIDAYS

2.6.3.1  That each party shall have
one of the first two days of [holiday A], alternating each year between the
first day and the second day;

2.6.3.2  That the Children will be
with the Plaintiff every [holiday B];

2.6.3.3  That for [holiday C], the
Plaintiff shall be entitled to have the Children with her for up to one half of
the holiday, at her discretion, the schedule to be fixed by the parties, acting
reasonably;

2.6.3.4  That each of the parties
shall have one of the first two days of [holiday F], alternating each year between
the first day and the second day. The parties may also choose to divide the
last two days of [holiday F];

2.6.4     SUMMER HOLIDAY PERIOD

2.6.4.1  That the parties shall
amicably divide the school summer holiday period;

2.6.4.2  That as of the 2008 summer
holiday period, and for no more than one month, the two older Children shall
attend sleep away camp;

2.6.4.3  That during the weeks that
the two older Children are away at sleep away camp, the parties shall each have
the remaining Children for periods of one week, on an alternating basis;

2.6.4.4  That once the two older
Children are home from camp and for the remainder of the summer holiday period,
the parties shall each have the Children for one period of two consecutive
weeks (for vacation purposes);

2.6.4.5
The summer schedule
shall be worked out between the parties acting reasonably;

2.6.4.6  The parties agree to
decide on camps, including day camp and sleep away camp by January of each
year. The summer schedule, including vacation time, is to be decided by June
1sl of each year;

2.6.4.7
That the Defendant
undertakes to register the Children in camps for the whole summer, including
morning and afternoon extended care, allowing the Plaintiff to work and to send
the Children to camp during her weeks of access;

2.7        DEFENDANT’S TRAVEL

2.7.1     That during the year,
Defendant is obliged to travel for work purposes;

2.7.2
That during such
periods of travel, the Children will remain with the Plaintiff, either at the
Defendant’s residence, if agreed to by the Defendant, or in the Plaintiffs
residence;

2.7.3
That during such
periods, Plaintiff will have the use of the Children’s nanny;

2.7.4     That Defendant agrees
that the periods of travel during which the Plaintiff shall be responsible for
the Children will be limited to three trips per year of no more than four days
and one trip of approximately two weeks per year to [Country A] (“Periods of
Travel”);

2.8        MEDICAL AND DENTAL
APPOINTMENTS

2.8.1     That until such time as
the Plaintiff is working, Plaintiff shall continue to bring the Children to
their appointments;

2.8.2     That once the Plaintiff
is working, Plaintiff will continue to bring the Children to their appointments
where possible;

2.9        BIRTHDAYS

2.9.1     That where possible, the
parties shall celebrate the Children’s birthdays together;

2.10      MOTHER’S DAY AND FATHER’S
DAY

2.10.1   That the Children shall be
with the Plaintiff on Mother’s Day and the Children shall be with the Defendant
on Father’s Day;

2.11      ADDITIONAL ACCESS

2.11.1   That it is the intention
of the parties to allow the Plaintiff to have as much additional access to the
Children as possible, including daily access to one or more of the Children,
for meals, activities or sleepovers;

2.11.2   That the Plaintiff shall
therefore be entitled to take one or more of the Children at any other time,
acting reasonably;

3.
EXPENSES RELATING TO
THE CHILDREN

3.1        That Defendant,
without contribution by Plaintiff, shall pay all of the expenses of the
Children, including, without limitation:

3.1.1     The cost of a nanny,
which nanny Plaintiff shall have access to during Periods of Travel;

3.1.2     All of the Children’s
school costs, including school fees if any, school supplies, books, uniform
costs and extended care;

That as long as the
Plaintiff is not working, she will be responsible for taking the Children for
their uniforms, school supplies and books (at Defendant’s cost). Once the
Plaintiff is working, the responsibly for taking the Children will be shared
with the Defendant;

3.1.3     All extracurricular
activities, the activities to be chosen by the parties, acting reasonably;

3.1.4     All clothing costs,
the Plaintiff to receive sufficient clothing from the Defendant to retain at
her residence;

The responsibility
for taking the Children to purchase clothing (at Defendant’s cost) shall shared
by the Plaintiff and the Defendant;

3.1.5     All camp costs,
including both morning and evening extended           care;

3.1.6     All medical and dental
costs, Defendant to maintain the Children on his group medical dental plan;

4.          JOURNAL

4.1        The parties will put in
place a journal, in which the parties shall indicate all of the Children's
activities and appointments, and other pertinent information pertaining to the
Children required by the parties;

4.2        The journal will include
all school activities, including parent teacher interviews and school programs;

5.          REPORT CARDS AND SCHOOL
ISSUES

5.1        That the parties will
also ensure that both parties obtain copies of the Children’s report cards and
are kept up to date on all school issues;

6.
CHILD SUPPORT

6.1        That except in the
event of a change in the residential schedule of the Children, and as long as
the Defendant is paying spousal support to the Plaintiff, no child support
shall be payable to Plaintiff for the times that the Children are with her;

6.2        That once the
Plaintiff is working, the parties agree that child support shall be calculated
in accordance with the Tables, the Child Support determination forms and the
parties then existing circumstances, the Plaintiffs revenues to be based on all
of her earnings (salary, interest and dividends, if any) excluding spousal
support
;

7.
SPOUSAL SUPPORT

7.1        That the Defendant,
in order to assist the Plaintiff, shall pay to the Plaintiff, alimentary
support for a period of five years only, namely from August 1st 2007 to July
31st 2012 (the “Period”), as follows:

7.2        For the period of
August 1st 2007 to July 31st 2010, the Defendant shall pay to the Plaintiff
alimentary support of $4,000.00 per month, without indexation;

7.3        For the period of
August 1st 2010 to July 31st 2012, the Defendant shall pay to the Plaintiff
alimentary support of $2,000.00 per month, without indexation;

7.4        That at the end of
the Period, no further alimentary support shall be paid to the Plaintiff,
regardless of the Plaintiffs circumstances;

7.5        That the Plaintiff
realizes that there may be future changes in her financial circumstances by
reason of her health, by reason of accident, the cost of living, her
employment, financial mismanagement, financial reversals, inheritance or
otherwise. No change whatsoever will give her the right to claim additional
support from the Defendant pursuant to the
Divorce Act
, the
Quebec Civil Code
,
or any law in Quebec or any other jurisdiction, even if the change is material,
profound, catastrophic, drastic, or is a radical one, whether or not the change
is foreseeable, foreseen, unforeseeable, or unforeseen, whether or not the
change has a causal connection to the marriage, and whether or not such change
arises from a pattern of economic dependency related to the marriage.

7.6        That during the
Period, and in order to encourage the Plaintiff to obtain full time employment,
all of her earnings, regardless of the amount, shall not be considered as
grounds to request a reduction of the alimentary support payable to the
Plaintiff;

7.7        That in addition to
the spousal support, and subject to the terms and conditions of the Defendant’s
group medical and dental plan, Defendant shall be obliged to maintain the
Plaintiff on his current group medical and dental plan and agrees to submit all
prescriptions, invoices, and receipts submitted to him by the Plaintiff, and to
reimburse to the Plaintiff any and all amounts reimbursed to him by his insurer
with respect to the said prescriptions, invoices and receipts; This will apply
until Defendant remarries.

8.          MISCELLANEOUS

8.1        That the parties declare
that for the purposes of the present Consent Agreement, and at their specific
request, the parties were both represented by Me Reisa Teitelbaum, the parties
having been previously represented by independent counsel, Plaintiff by Me
Linda Schachter and Defendant by Me Andrew Heft, who have not advised the
parties regarding the contents of this agreement.

8.2        That the parties declare
having had the opportunity of having the present Consent Agreement reviewed by
separate and independent counsel and having chosen not to do so;

(emphasis added)

[
19
]

At the time of the signing of the 2007 Final
Consent, the parties were no longer represented by independent counsel, however
they were assisted by Me Teitelbaum, who was called to testify before the
undersigned by the Father, as will be discussed below.

[
20
]

As set out in the 2007 Final Consent, the joint
custody arrangement in place since the parties’ separation was maintained, with
a residential schedule corresponding loosely to 60% residency at the Father’s (weekdays
during school) and 40% residency at the Mother’s (extended weekends, summer
vacations and the like). Furthermore, the Father undertook to pay all expenses
of the children,
to the exclusion of the Mother
, as appears from
paragraph 3.1 which reads: “
That Defendant, without contribution by
Plaintiff, shall pay all of the expenses of the Children, including, without
limitation
…”. He also undertook to pay spousal support until July 31
st
,
2012 (paragraph 7), and the Mother renounced to any additional spousal support
after that date.

[
21
]

As for child support, paragraph 6 of the 2007
Final Consent appears to contemplate only the payment of child support
to
the Mother
and this, only if the residential schedule of the children
changes and only once spousal support has ceased. No child support payable
to
the Father
was contemplated by the 2007 Final Consent. The Court will
return to this issue below, as the Father has been claiming child support since
2008.

[
22
]

The 2007 Final Consent, homologated by the Court
on July 12
th
, 2007, did not halt the proceedings for very long.

[
23
]

Eight months later, on May 30
th
,
2008, the Father presented a new motion, this time claiming child support to be
paid to him by the Mother on an interim and provisional basis (the “Father’s
2008 Motion for child support”). His 2008 Motion for child support which was
accompanied by a Schedule I, indicating that his annual income was
$214,000 and indicating zero income for the Mother, who was still, as at that
date, receiving monthly spousal support. While he was claiming child support,
the Father did not request sole custody of the children in this 2008 Motion,
nor did he contest the joint custody residential schedule agreed to in the 2007
Final Consent.

[
24
]

On June 17
th
, 2008, when both parties
were unrepresented, Justice Danielle Richer refused the Father’s 2008 Motion
for child support on an interim basis for lack of urgency:

The demand for interim order is
denied for lack of urgency and the Court:

Strongly recommend the parties to
go to mediation;

The
parties will have to complete their files and namely the mother will have
deposit a document from her employer establishing her present income and
produce her child support determination form.

[
25
]

On June 26
th
, 2008, the Father, still
self-represented, filed a motion to vary Accessory measures (the “Father’s 2008
Motion to vary accessory measures”), in which he alleged that “
the Consent
Agreement provides for child support to be paid by the plaintiff once receiving
income
” (paragraph 5). He claimed that the Mother was working for the “
[Company
A]
” and asked for “
child support to be paid by the Plaintiff to
compensate for the unreasonable burden of full parental responsibility of four
children
”, based upon her notional income from this company, noting that
the Mother was not fully exercising her access rights. On August 20
th
,
2009, the Mother presented her Schedule I in response to the Father’s 2008
Motions, which indicated zero revenue for herself and $300,000 annual revenue
for the Father.

[
26
]

On July 14
th
, 2009 and on August 10
th
,
2009, Justice Francine Nantel rendered two judgments postponing the hearing on
the Father’s two 2008 Motions and ordering the parties to exchange information
with respect to their revenues for 2009.

[
27
]

The case was postponed until August 21
st
,
2009, on which date Justice Kirkland Casgrain continued the Father’s two
pending Motions
sine die
and ordered a psychosocial expertise,
stating the following:

Il est nécessaire que l’expertise
soit faite pour déterminer s’il doit y avoir des changements au niveau de la
garde; les enfants, en particulier, doivent avoir la possibilité de faire
valoir leur point de vue;

POUR CES MOTIFS
, les parties ont consenti à une expertise psychosociale et dans
l’intervalle le Tribunal
ORDONNE
que les parties respectent le document
intitulé « Consent Agreement », daté du 10 juillet 2007, l’affaire
est reportée sine die.

[
28
]

Dominic D’Abate, Ph.D., social worker, issued a 20 page
psychosocial report on October 23
rd
, 2009 (the “Expert’s Report
2009”), in which he recommended that joint custody continue; he also made several
comments concerning the impact of the conflict between the parents on the
children, as will be seen below.

[
29
]

On April 8
th
, 2010, the Mother presented
a motion to vary accessory measures (the Mother’s 2010 Motion to vary accessory
measures”), asking for full custody of the children commencing May 1
st
,
2010; child support in accordance with the tables based upon the Father’s earnings
of $300,000 per year; services of the nanny working for the Father and spousal
support of $7,500 per month, retroactive to the date of the Father’s Motion to
vary accessory measures.

[
30
]

On May 6
th
, 2010, when the Mother was
represented by Me Patricia Chamoun and the Father was self-represented, Justice
Piché, seized with the case management of the various pending Motions to vary
accessory measures, stated the following:

DÉCISION

Les parties ont été référées devant
le Tribunal pour un problème de gestion.

Monsieur se représente lui-même.
Madame est représentée par procureure, qui désire que Monsieur complète une
déclaration pour fixation d’un procès de 2 jours et plus. Dans la déclaration,
on parle de 2 jours d’audience nécessaires et la procureure parle de son propre
témoignage, de son conjoint, de l’administratrice de l’école des enfants, d’une
travailleuse sociale, d’amis de la famille et de la nanny des enfants.

Monsieur parle du fait qu’il
voudrait faire une requête afin de faire rejeter cette nouvelle demande de
Madame. Il s’agit d’une requête pour changement de garde, détermination de
pension alimentaire, une pension alimentaire pour Madame de 7 500 $
par mois, et une demande de payer des taxes rétroactives ainsi que des demandes
au sujet des dépenses médicales pour les enfants, etc.

10. Summary and Professional
Opinion

Mr. P. L. and Mrs. Y. M. were
married in 1991 and separated in 2004 at which time they made tentative plans
between them to share in the care of their four children. Constant
disagreements and difficulties in coordinating their parenting responsibilities
forced them to formulate a new and more detailed custodial arrangement which
was signed in July, 2007. Unfortunately, this new agreement proved no less easy
to implement, and on August 21, 2009 the couple found themselves in front of
the Honorable Judge Kirkland Casgrain who requested that a psychosocial
assessment be undertaken to assist the court in determining “How is the consent
agreement - dated July 10, 2007 applied by the parties and what is in the best
interest of the parties’ children”, as well as to whether there needs to be any
change with regards to the question of custody. As such, the recommendations
contained in this report are based primarily on interviews conducted with all
significant parties and take into account the following considerations;

1.          The children were seen
on two occasions, with their parents and alone. As requested by the honourable
judge, they were interviewed together and individually in order to give them
the possibility of expressing their views and opinion with regards to the
present custodial arrangement. While care was taken in not making them feel
that they had to choose between their parents, they were asked to relate their
level of comfort with their past and present living arrangements. They were
also queried as to what they most desired at the family level and what would
best meet their respective needs.

In general, the answers all four
children provided were in keeping with those of most children their age
experiencing the divorce of their parents: wanting their parents to come back
together as a couple, to live close to each other, collaborate more and, most
of all, to stop fighting . They all feel quite comfortable with the present
living arrangement as they enjoy being with their father, feel secure and enjoy
a certain degree of comfort and convenience with regards to having their own
room, being close to their school and having friends in the neighbourhood. At
the same time, it is evident that they are also very attached to their mother
with whom they have and want to continue having a close relationship. All four
children expressed a desire to see her more, especially the younger children
who appear to need a regular and frequent contact with her.

2.          Mr. L. and Mrs. M.
spent a great deal of time in our interviews trying to present the other parent
(by verbal persuasion or documented proof) as being either incompetent or
irresponsible in their parenting role. In fact, given the sheer volume of the
court file, both parties appear to have been locked into this pattern of
interaction for some time. Over the years, there have been numerous legal and
mental health professionals who, in good faith, have become part of this
litigious process and, unwittingly, contributed to a spiralling conflict that
appears to have no end in sight. As such, the intention of this expert is not
to acquiesce to the parents’ perceived need to prove their superiority over the
other but, rather, to focus, as requested by the court, on what is in the best
interest of the four minor children and on implementing a parenting plan (e.g.
consent agreement of 2007) that would meet their needs.

3.          Both Mr. L. and Mrs. M.
do love and care for their children and have sufficient strengths as parents to
be able to, ideally, carry out a parenting plan (consent agreement) with
optimum collaboration and flexibility and minimal rancorous vindictive
interactions. Certainly, there does not seem to be any obvious reason why two
intelligent and well intentioned parents who both admit they need to
collaborate with each other have been compelled to engage in such protracted
conflict, especially knowing that their children do not benefit from or
appreciate their constant fighting and lack of cooperation. One can only
speculate that unresolved couple issues, personal dispositions and the
circumstances in which they find themselves continue to motivate and direct
their actions and thinking. The scope and intent of this report does not permit
for more detailed analysis of the possible influence of these factors on the
present situation. That being said, it is very clear, however, that it is
incumbent on each of them to engage (perhaps with the help of a professional)
in some serious reflection of their own behaviour and the consequences that it
is having on the well being of their children.

4.          With regards to the
difficulties encountered in the implementation of the 2007 consent agreement
between the two parents, several elements and developments need to be taken into
consideration:

a)         Although the agreement
was finalized following a long period of negotiation, it appears that Mrs. M.,
by her admission, has not totally bought into the plan or custody arrangement
and feels that Mr. L. has not kept, according to her, certain commitments made
to her. This has resulted in her less than enthusiastic participation in
applying its provision which are detailed enough and clear in the
responsibilities assigned to each parent.

b)         Both parents have a
tendency to scrutinize and interpret every action taken by the other parent in
an overly critical manner. Consequently, each easily finds faults and questions
decisions made with regards to how their parental responsibilities are being
carried out. This lack of mutual respect and trust makes it difficult for them
to engage in a co-parenting relationship and effectively implement any plan or
judgement.

c)         There has been a
breakdown in the ability and willingness of both parents to discuss matters
related to the children and exchange important information with regards to the
latter’s activities, functioning and whereabouts. It is difficult if not
impossible to implement a co-parenting or ‘joint custody’ arrangement under
these conditions unless outside assistance is utilized to help bridge the gap.
This expert feels strongly that it is in the children’s best interest for the
parents to take any measure necessary to ensure that they remain, both,
actively involved in their lives.

5.
Given the fact that
it is in the best interest of the children that a co-parenting (joint custody)
arrangement be maintained and given the aforementioned discussion on the
difficulties in implementing such a plan, it is strongly recommended that Mr. L.
and Mrs. M. seek professional help to assist them to function more effectively
as two parents.
Firstly, both parents should sit down with a family
mediator and discuss how the existing consent agreement can become more
responsive to the needs of all concerned (they have changed some provisions
already). This does not necessarily mean a major revision or scrapping the
existing agreement unless both parents feel it is necessary to do so. Mrs. M.
needs to accept and commit herself to any revised agreement and ensure that she
faithfully carries out her stipulated obligations and responsibilities. As
well, she must accept the fact that Mr. L. has a personal and social life and
that he needs time to himself without the children and that she cannot simply
decide, arbitrarily, when and how she sees her children. Mr. L., for his part,
needs to be sensitive to the fact that Mrs. M. now feels marginalized in
her parenting role and he must make every effort not to make her feel as an

Secondly, that the parents agree to
have the court appoint a Parenting Coordinator (PC)
[…]
that will
assist them (counselling, mediation, coaching, decision making) in successfully
implementing a final parenting plan. The professional engaged as a PC should
also be given, by the parents, the right to make a binding decision in those
situations where the parents are at odds with how an aspect of the parenting
plan should be carried out and are unable to find a compromise. As well, the PC
would help the parents focus on the best interest of the children and would
intervene to help resolve a dispute involving them. While the appointment of a
PC has been limited in Quebec, it has not been without precedent and has been

5.

It is clear that the Father would have paid

[

support, retroactive to 2012 and without a term, is also dismissed.

[

]

She initially made a claim for increased spousal
support in her 2010 Motion to vary accessory measures, in which she asked for
full custody, child support and increased spousal support of $7,500 per month
retroactive to the filing of the Father’s 2009 Motion to vary accessory
measures. This claim was dismissed by Justice Perrault, who re-confirmed the
parties’ 2007 Final Consent of 2007, in which the Mother renounced to any claim
for spousal support after July 31
st
, 2012 (paragraph 7.3),
notwithstanding any future changes in her financial circumstances or otherwise
(paragraph 7.5).

[
96
]

As a result, this issue has been decided by the
Superior Court, like the issue of child support, and the law between the
parties remains their 2007 Final Consent in which the Mother renounces to
spousal support after 2012.

[
97
]

Furthermore, the jurisprudence militates against
the variation of such a renunciation to spousal support except in very rare
circumstances, for instance in the event of a radical change which was not
predictable and which was linked to the marriage
[1]
.
No evidence was offered by the Mother of such a radical change linked to the
marriage, although as noted, the Father’s alienating behaviour and insistence
on re-litigating the issue of child support may be sufficient to justify her
claim in damages.

Claim by Mother for
reimbursement of expenses and damages

[
98
]

Several of the Mother’s claims for reimbursement
of expenses are well-founded. In particular, the Father owes the Mother $6,000
in medical claims collected by him from his insurance and not reimbursed to
her. The Father also owes an amount to the Mother representing summer camp
expenses he had undertaken to pay in the 2007 Final Consent, and which he never
paid, along with similar holiday expenses and the cost of the nanny. However,
these expenses are difficult to quantify in the circumstances, as when the
Father failed to provide the camps and the nanny, the children stayed with him.

[
99
]

Articles 51 and following of the
Code of
civil procedure
(“C.c.p.”) deal with abusive procedures and allow the Court
to declare a proceeding abusive on its own initiative and also to award damages
and legal costs. The pertinent articles read as follows:

51
.
The
courts may, at any time, on an application and even on their own initiative,
declare that a judicial application or a pleading is abusive
.

Regardless of intent, the abuse of
procedure may consist in
a judicial application or pleading that is clearly
unfounded, frivolous or intended to delay or in conduct that is vexatious or
quarrelsome
. It may also consist in a
use of procedure that is excessive
or unreasonable or that causes prejudice to another person
, or attempts to
defeat the ends of justice, particularly if it operates to restrict another
person’s freedom of expression in public debate.

54
. On
ruling on whether a judicial application or pleading, including one presented
under this division, is abusive,
the court may
order a provision for
costs to be reimbursed,
order a party to pay, in addition to legal costs,
damages for any injury suffered by another party, including to cover the
professional fees and disbursements incurred by that other party, or award
punitive damages if warranted by the circumstances
.

If the amount of the damages is
not admitted or cannot be easily calculated at the time the application or
pleading is declared abusive, the court may summarily determine the amount
within the time and subject to the conditions it specifies or, in
the case of the Court of Appeal, refer the matter back to the court of first
instance for a decision.

55.
If
an abuse of procedure results from a party’s quarrelsomeness,
the court may,
in addition to other measures, prohibit the party from instituting a judicial
application or presenting a pleading in an ongoing proceeding except with the
authorization of and subject to the conditions determined by the chief justice
or the chief judge
.

(emphasis added)

[
100
]

The Mother, in her 2016 Motions, asks the Court
to declare that the Father’s proceedings, including his repeated claims for
child support, are abusive. The Court agrees. The Father’s repeated requests to
vary accessory measures and for child support, commencing in November 2007,
three months after signing the 2007 Final Consent, were clearly unfounded,
frivolous and indeed abusive, especially given his attempts to prevent the
children from spending residential time with their Mother, to their detriment,
so that he could claim that he had “de facto” sole custody, as he claimed
before the undersigned.

[
101
]

The Court therefore declares the Father’s 2016
Motion to vary accessory measures abusive, pursuant to article 51 C.c.p. Given
the abusive and frivolous nature of the Father’s Motions and claims in this
file, over the course of the last 12 years, the Mother’s claim for damages is
well-founded and although the quantification of such damages is difficult,
article 54 C.p.c. allows the Court to summarily determine the amount of such
damages.

[
102
]

The undersigned is of the view that the Father
should pay the Mother damages in the amount of $25,000, representing
compensation for all of the expenses for which he was responsible under the
2007 Final Consent and which he declined to contribute, including the cost of
the nanny, summer camps, clothing, uniforms, etc., and his actions which led to
the children gradually staying primarily with him.

[
103
]

Furthermore, the Father must pay the Mother’s
legal fees and disbursements of $7,000, pursuant to article 54 C.c.p., which
are substantiated by the evidence.

[
104
]

In conclusion, the Court makes the following
comments.

[
105
]

These self-represented litigants have pursued
their judicial guerilla warfare since their separation in 2004. In 2009, ten
years ago, the expert had already chastised the parties and noted that their
conflicts were proving to be detrimental not only to them but to their
children. There have been approximately 11 days of hearings on the merits since
2007, countless days in practice court over the last 12 years and 7-8 case
management hearings, the whole largely with respect to motions which had either
already been litigated, as noted above, or which were simply ill-founded in
fact and in law. Nevertheless, the Superior Court has, without exception, been
exceeding indulgent in assisting these self-represented parties in presenting
their case.

[
106
]

However, it stops now. The children are almost
all majors, and becoming independent. The parties have re-made their lives.
They must learn to communicate with each other in a positive way, so that in
the future, they can both attend together the happy occasions that are sure to
arise in the lives of their children. In order to do so, they must learn to
deal with their differences reasonably and should attend, along with the
children who wish to do so, family therapy and/or counseling for which they
will each pay 50% of the cost.

[
107
]

The Court therefore declares that these parties
are quarrelsome litigants pursuant to article 55 C.c.p. and will prohibit them
from instituting a judicial application or presenting a pleading with respect
to their marriage, divorce and children without the authorization of the Chief
Justice or the Associate Chief Justice.
